findings: The review begins from the current single source Question and Canonical ownership, not from the contaminated long-tail baseline; the preserved source only requires counting index pairs whose a[i] + reverse(a[i]) values are equal.

The first isolated audit correctly rejected revision 1 because its displayed Java block contained methods without a compilable class. Revision 2 embeds the complete ReverseSumPairs class and removes that coding hard failure without changing the algorithm contract.

The candidate answers the relation directly by projecting each element to x + reverse(x), grouping online with a frequency map, and adding the prior frequency so each i<j pair is counted exactly once.

The candidate clearly separates source facts from executable-example assumptions: non-negative int input, decimal integer reverse semantics, i<j pair ordering, null rejection, Java language choice, and long storage are declared candidate contracts rather than attributed to the source.

The Java fixture compiles and passes empty/singleton cases, one and three same-key pairs, all-zero combinations, two independent equal-key groups, leading-zero integer reversal, a reversed 32-bit value exceeding int, and explicit undefined null/negative boundaries.
The mechanism section supplies the grouping invariant and C(m,2) argument, the answer states O(n*d) time and O(n) extra space, and the sorting alternative explains the principal time/space tradeoff.

Follow-ups are specific to pair counting, reverse semantics, overflow and the sorting variant; the answer fabricates no project history and contains no unrelated Java equals/hashCode material from the legacy baseline.

No uncovered source variant, unsupported source attribution, coding hard failure, or semantic blocker remains in revision 2. Formal promotion remains subject to repository promotion and real-review policy.
